name: Water cutting / dehydration pre-photo

card.summary: Restricting fluids to look drier or sharper for a photo; dehydration has well-documented health risks.
card.note: Dehydration impairs cognition and can be dangerous at larger losses.

quick.overview:
Water cutting means deliberately limiting fluids, sometimes alongside other measures, shortly before a photo, show or weigh-in so the body looks drier and more defined. It originates in physique sport and is sometimes discussed in appearance communities.

No studies of its effect on appearance were found, while the health effects of dehydration are well documented.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say less water under the skin and in tissues gives a tighter, more defined look. Body water loss reduces blood volume and tissue hydration.
quick.risks: Medical sources report that losing 1 to 2 percent of body water can impair thinking, 5 to 8 percent can cause fatigue and dizziness, and losses above 10 percent can cause serious decline. Reference material links intentional dehydration to higher death rates among bodybuilders.

lead: Water cutting, or pre-photo dehydration, is the practice of limiting fluid intake in the hours or days before a photograph, contest or weigh-in so the body looks drier and more defined. Its stated aim is to reduce the water held under the skin so that muscle separation, vascularity and the jawline and abdominal outlines show more sharply.[1][2]

The practice comes from competitive bodybuilding. In the final stage of contest preparation, competitors combine carbohydrate loading with dehydration, and a 2021 review in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation describes the goal as keeping intramuscular water and glycogen while reducing subcutaneous (extracellular) water, so an athlete looks "dry" rather than "watery."[1][2] In a survey of 81 natural bodybuilders cited in that review, 65.4 percent reported water loading and 32.1 percent reported water restriction.[2]

The same review states that current evidence does not show the practices to be specifically effective or safe, and that coaching protocols have not been scientifically evaluated; in one study the bodybuilders themselves judged their water manipulation largely ineffective.[2] Medical references describe dehydration as causing thirst, headache, fatigue and reduced urination, with effects on thinking from losses of 1 to 2 percent of body water.[3]

chain: Fluid intake limited before a photo or show
Less water held under the skin
Skin looks tighter, muscle outlines and veins show more
angle.text: Competitors and some photo-minded lifters restrict water in the last stage of a cut so that skin lies closer to muscle and definition shows. A 2021 review notes that the main supporting data come from a study in combat athletes, and that its authors consider the practice unevaluated for physique appearance.[2]

infobox: 32.1% water restriction among 81 natural bodybuilders surveyed[2]

paras: Competitors cut fat for roughly 12 to 14 weeks and, in the last stage, combine carbohydrate loading with dehydration to improve definition and vascularity.[1] Some people outside competition adopt short fluid restriction before photos. Specific protocols are not described here.

The 2021 review by Escalante, Stevenson, Barakat, Aragon and Schoenfeld notes that glycogen loading draws water into muscle, so water intake is typically matched to carbohydrate loading, and cites earlier work in which extracellular and intracellular water losses during dehydration approach a 1:1 ratio once glycogen stabilizes.[2]

No studies found measuring water cutting for photographic appearance. The 2021 peak-week review reports that the main supporting data for water loading followed by restriction come from a study in combat athletes, in which body water fell without reported harm, and that bodybuilders in another study judged their water manipulation largely ineffective.[2]

Symptoms include thirst, headache, nausea, less frequent urination, dry mucous membranes and dizziness on standing. Losses of about 3 to 4 percent of body water are usually tolerated, 5 to 8 percent can cause fatigue and dizziness, more than 10 percent brings serious physical and mental decline, and 15 to 25 percent can be fatal. Complications include hypernatremia, kidney problems, heatstroke, seizures and hypovolemic shock.[3]

The peak-week review describes a case report of a bodybuilder who drank very large daily volumes of water for a week, together with a diuretic and salt restriction, and developed electrolyte disturbances, water intoxication and rhabdomyolysis; he recovered after treatment.[2] A survey of 382 competitors reported frequent sodium depletion and dehydration in the days before competition.[2] The authors suggest that leaving these variables alone may be a better option for some competitors and that miscalculated manipulation can cause a competitor to miss their peak or develop health problems.[2] Reference material links intentional dehydration to higher mortality among bodybuilders.[1]

timeline.event: Review of peak-week practices published in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation.[2]

lore.intro: Water cutting is discussed in physique and lean-look communities as a last-minute step for photos and contests.

claims.claim: Dehydrating makes you look sharper in photos
claims.believers: Proponents say the skin looks tighter and muscles more visible, and bodybuilding coaches have long used water and sodium manipulation in contest week.[2]
claims.experts: The 2021 review states that current evidence does not show these practices to be specifically effective, and that no coaching protocols have been scientifically evaluated.[2]

claims.claim: A short water cut has no meaningful downside
claims.believers: Some users call it harmless if brief.
claims.experts: Dehydration of 1 to 2 percent can impair thinking and severe loss can be fatal;[3] the review describes a case report of serious harm from combined water, diuretic and salt manipulation.[2]
